title: Did Nobunaga Really Say "Kill It"? The Cuckoo Verses' Own Source Says They're Made Up
description:
On Bunsei 4, 11th month, 17th day (Dec. 11, 1821, Gregorian), a kasshi day, Hirado's retired lord Matsura Seizan began the Kasshi Yawa that night. Volume 53: someone sends a cuckoo (hototogisu) that won't sing; before the three verses, a remark from the night talk: "probably falsely attributed, but it fits these three men's natures well." The verses are signed with titles; two added ones name no author.

The earliest found so far is the Mimibukuro of Negishi Yasumori (died Bunka 12, 1815): the three sit together, Ieyasu says "when it sings, I'll listen," and Jōha adds "that's fine too"; Negishi doesn't know if it's an old tale or made up. Post-Meiji books nearly all call it invented, yet the wording kept changing: in 1909 Ieyasu's line read "naku made matō," by 1910 all three neared today's, and a 1935 ethics guide quoting the Kasshi Yawa changed 待よ to 俟てよ. Which book fixed today's version, we did not find; who wrote the verses is still unknown.

Kasshi Yawa: the Matsuras' Meiji 33 edition (NIJL, text only); Mimibukuro: six-volume Nihon Geirin Sōsho; later books: NDL Digital. We didn't open the Tōyō Bunko or ten-volume editions (wording may differ); Ieyasu's testament: secondary sources only; "found so far" means within our search. Narrated dates are lunar; "we think" is this channel's view.

AI-generated illustrations; historical figures are unnamed cartoons, not likenesses; the bird stays unharmed.

Data as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

k101.text: You've surely heard it: if the cuckoo won't sing, Nobunaga kills it, Hideyoshi coaxes it to sing, Ieyasu waits.

k102.text: Three verses, one bird: for 200 years, people read these men's natures in them.

k103.text: Bunsei 4, 11th month, 17th day: Hirado's retired lord Matsura Seizan talks with a guest till late.

k104.text: He began writing that night, a kasshi day; hence its name, Kasshi Yawa.

k105.text: In it, someone sends a cuckoo, the bird called hototogisu, and it won't make a sound.

k106.text: But before the verses, Seizan records a remark: probably falsely attributed.

k108.text: Stranger still: in another shogunate official's notes, Ieyasu says a different line.

k110.text: This file follows the bird from a night talk in Bunsei 4 to a classroom in Shōwa 10.

k111.text: Did Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu really write these?

k201.text: So who said it? Turn to volume 53, leaf 7: it says only "aru hito," someone, speaking during the night talk.

k202.text: That remark goes on: "but it fits these three men's natures well."

k203.text: Falsely attributed: made up under another's name. The speaker isn't Seizan; he just noted what he heard.

k204.text: It threw me the first time I read this: the most-quoted source says up front it's made up. What is this book?

k205.text: We read the Matsura family's own print of the 100-volume main set, Meiji 33.

k206.text: Seizan wrote it only after retiring, one entry at a time, nearly 300 volumes in all;

k208.text: The cuckoo entry sits amid hundreds of chats; neither entry next to it is on the three.

k209.text: Only after that remark come the bird and the verses. Who was it sent to?

k210.text: Who got it, and when, isn't written; and if you're looking for the three at one table, it's not here.

k211.text: The verses aren't signed Nobunaga, Hideyoshi or Ieyasu, either. So what are they signed?

k212.text: Three titles. Oda Ufu: Won't sing? Then kill it.

k213.text: Hō Taikō: Silent? Make it sing for me to see.

k214.text: Dai Gongen-sama: Won't sing? Then wait till it sings.

k215.text: Ufu means Minister of the Right; Dai Gongen, Ieyasu's title as a god after death.

k216.text: Even its name varies: the bird has many kanji; "season bird," "cuckoo," "kakkō" all mean it.

k217.text: One much-quoted copy uses three spellings in three verses; and our Meiji edition?

k218.text: The proofreader's afterword: doubtful characters were fixed only after checking sources, asking friends.

k219.text: The proofreading took 28 months. Keep this proofreader in mind.

k220.text: But that's not all: two more verses follow.

k221.text: One says: Won't sing? Send it to the bird shop. The other: Won't sing? Just keep it.

k222.text: The book: out of caution, and as it was falsely attributed anyway, no author is named. Who are those two about?

k223.text: The book says nothing. I suspect you're as curious as I am, but with no source, we won't guess.

k224.text: So was Seizan the first to record these three men and this bird?

k301.text: No. The earliest found so far is that shogunate official from the start: Negishi Yasumori.

k302.text: He died in Bunka 12, when not one word of Seizan's night talks had been written yet.

k303.text: Starting as Sado magistrate, he took notes for about 30 years: Mimibukuro.

k304.text: This entry's title: At a renga gathering, a person's true heart shows on its own.

k306.text: Old tale or someone's invention, I don't know.

k307.text: Two books, two recorders, and each opens with a disclaimer. That's odd: both say they're unsure, yet the verses still spread.

k309.text: The three meet: it's the 4th month, and no cuckoo has sung yet.

k310.text: The old 4th month is about today's May, when cuckoos are due; each early summer, Edo waited for the first call.

k311.text: If it stayed silent in its season, you'd probably want to say something to it too.

k312.text: Nobunaga speaks first, and his line means the same as in Seizan's record.

k313.text: Hideyoshi says: Silent? Make it sing for me to hear. Seizan's differs at the end: there, "to see"; here, "to hear."

k314.text: Negishi leaves a blank before Ieyasu, out of respect. And what of Ieyasu?

k315.text: Won't sing? When it sings, I'll listen.

k316.text: This line has no "wait"; that "wait" appears only in Seizan's entry.

k317.text: I think it's a big gap: waiting is endurance; listening when it sings is more like letting it be.

k318.text: Beside them sat Jōha, the era's top renga poet, who added a fourth verse:

k320.text: Negishi says the verses show each man's nature: Ieyasu gentle, Hideyoshi generous, Nobunaga hot-tempered.

k321.text: So before Seizan started writing, how far had these verses spread?

k401.text: Far enough to change the head count. In the Meiji 10s, someone hand-copied an old essay that even adds Maeda Toshiie;

k402.text: The setting: Nobunaga's banquet at Azuchi Castle, and beside each verse, one character: courage, loyalty, wisdom, benevolence.

k403.text: It doesn't say which essay it came from; so we can only say a four-man version existed before early Meiji.

k404.text: But that's not all: some made a joke of it. A Taishō-era senryū scholar placed one senryū in the Bunka era:

k405.text: One cuckoo, turned into three verses: wisdom, benevolence, courage.

k406.text: If that date is right, the verses had reached commoners' senryū before Seizan wrote;

k407.text: Which came first, it or Mimibukuro? Unclear.

k408.text: See? This far in, three men have become four, and we're on a third setting.

k408b.text: I think it's less a record than a joke going around.

k409.text: So in Meiji, did books still say it may be made up?

k501.text: They still did. In Meiji 34, a self-cultivation book wrote: "Probably a tale made up by someone."

k502.text: Yet it adds: from these verses, you can imagine the three men's characters.

k503.text: It also writes "naku," sing, with the kanji for weeping, and signs them by real name.

k504.text: I find this step neat: Seizan's still had three titles; here they're three real names. And books for kids?

k505.text: In Meiji 37, a primary-school textbook dictionary labeled them "on Nobunaga," "on Hideyoshi," "on Ieyasu": comments about them.

k507.text: Life is like a long journey with a heavy burden; never hurry.

k509.text: You've likely heard it too; in the same entry as the verses, it entered a primary teachers' handbook.

k510.text: So when did today's verses take this shape?

k601.text: In Meiji 42, a youth self-cultivation book also said: a later fabrication, but each verse nails its man.

k602.text: But the wording kept changing: here the three meet and wait a long time, and the bird won't sing.

k603.text: Ieyasu's line already reads "I'll wait till it sings," like today. What about the other two?

k604.text: In Meiji 43, a speech and writing guide for the sixth-grade reader wrote out the three verses,

k605.text: and they read almost exactly like today's.

k606.text: This book, too, says only: legend has it these three wrote them.

k607.text: So the set you can recite isn't from those two Edo books; it's from late-Meiji classrooms.

k608.text: But that's not the last setting. In Taishō 15, the man who placed that senryū in the Bunka era noted another view:

k609.text: Probably later people depicting the three via the cuckoo.

k610.text: In his version, the scene shifts again: a poetry meet with a preset theme;

k610b.text: each name tagged: man of courage, man of wisdom, man of benevolence.

k611.text: I counted: by now the setting has changed four times; this story really loves a costume change.

k612.text: So which book fixed today's version?

k701.text: We couldn't find such a book. The opening "if it won't sing" alone has six spellings.

k702.text: That year a middle-school ethics lesson used it, titled "The Waiting Heart."

k703.text: Section 1: Someone tells of the minds of Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu. Still "someone."

k704.text: The teachers' guide cites the Kasshi Yawa, quoting even the two added verses and "no author is named."

k706.text: No. In Ieyasu's line, "wait" took the kanji from the lesson's title; in Hideyoshi's signature, "Tai" got a new kanji too.

k707.text: Remember that Meiji proofreader? He changed characters to make them right; this time, to match a lesson title.

k708.text: If you sat in that class, the Ieyasu you heard was this one who "waits."

k709.text: Five years later, a national history reader was blunter: three Sengoku heroes would never cozy up to write on one bird.

k710.text: He says it must be a later fabrication.

k711.text: And the "long journey with a heavy burden," set beside the verses in Meiji 37?

k712.text: Researchers think it got Ieyasu's name only in late Edo;

k712b.text: Around Meiji 11, someone added Ieyasu's signature and cipher to it and offered it at Nikkō's Tōshōgū.

k713.text: So, back to the opening question: did they write these three verses?

k714.text: Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu died in 1582, 1598 and 1616;

k715.text: That's the 200 years from the start: the two Edo notebooks found so far both came about 200 years after them.

k716.text: No record from their own time mentions these verses.

k717.text: Who really wrote them is still unknown today.

k718.text: Remember the night talk's "it fits these three men's natures well"? We think that likeness is what spread them.

k719.text: None of the three verses are theirs. File archived.

k720.text: Which line for this silent bird? Tell me in the comments.

k721.text: This channel sticks to the records. Subscribe to open the files with me.
